module_title: Packaging and Branding Your Dried Products

lessons.title: Choosing Affordable and Attractive Packaging
lessons.body: When choosing packaging for your dried fruits and vegetables, you need to balance cost, protection, and appeal. In most African markets, the cheapest option is clear plastic bags (poly bags) with a thickness of 0.05mm to 0.08mm. A pack of 100 bags sized 15cm x 20cm costs about $2 to $3 in local markets or from suppliers like Alibaba. These are fine for local sales but not for long storage because they let in air and moisture. For better shelf life, use laminated pouches with a foil or metallized layer. These cost $0.10 to $0.30 each when bought in 1000s, but they keep products fresh for 6-12 months. You can find them from packaging suppliers in Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra. Another affordable option is glass jars with metal lids, which are reusable and attractive for gifts, but they are heavier and cost $0.50 to $1 each. For urban customers, stand-up pouches with a zip lock are popular and look professional. They cost $0.20 to $0.40 each. Always buy in bulk to reduce unit cost. For example, buying 5000 pouches can cut the price by 30%. Also consider the size: 50g, 100g, and 200g are common. Smaller sizes sell faster in low-income areas. Make sure the packaging is food-grade and has a tight seal. Avoid recycled plastic that may have odors. Test your packaging by filling it with your product and leaving it for a week to see if moisture gets in. Attractive packaging includes clear windows to show the product, bright colors, and a simple design. You can add a sticker with your brand name. Remember, packaging is your silent salesman. Even a simple clear bag with a well-designed label can boost sales by 20% compared to plain bags. So invest wisely: start with affordable clear bags for local markets, and upgrade to laminated pouches as your profits grow.

lessons.title: Sealing and Labeling for Longer Shelf Life
lessons.body: Proper sealing is critical to keep your dried products crispy and free from mold. The most common method is heat sealing. You can buy a simple impulse sealer for $20 to $50 from online stores or local suppliers. It uses a heating element to melt the plastic layers together. For poly bags, set the sealer to medium heat (2-3 seconds). For laminated pouches, use higher heat (3-4 seconds). Always test on a spare bag. If the seal is weak, increase time or temperature. Another method is using a zip lock, but these are not airtight for long storage. For glass jars, ensure the lid has a rubber gasket and screw it tight. After sealing, check for leaks by squeezing the bag gently; if air escapes, reseal. For labeling, you must include: product name, ingredients, net weight, production date, expiry date, and your contact. Use a permanent marker or printed stickers. A roll of 500 stickers costs $5 to $10. Expiry date: dried fruits last 6-12 months if sealed well. For example, dried mango at 10% moisture can last 12 months in a foil pouch. Write the date clearly: "Best before: Dec 2025". Also include storage instructions: "Store in a cool, dry place". For export, you need batch numbers and nutrition facts, but for local markets, simple labels are fine. Labeling helps you track your production and builds trust. If a customer complains, you can trace the batch. Also, labeling with your phone number allows reorders. A good practice is to seal and label immediately after drying and cooling, because moisture from the air can re-enter. Work in a dry room. Use a hair dryer on cool setting to remove any surface moisture before sealing. Always wear gloves to avoid contaminating the product. With proper sealing and labeling, your products can stay fresh for months, reducing waste and increasing profits.

lessons.title: Designing a Simple Brand Name and Logo
lessons.body: Your brand name and logo are the face of your business. Start by choosing a name that is easy to remember, pronounce, and spell. Avoid long names. Use words that reflect your product or region, like "Savanna Dry", "Mango Gold", or "Zuri Fruits". Check if the name is already used by searching online or at your local business registry. You can register a business name for about $20 to $50 in many African countries. For the logo, you don't need a professional designer. You can use free tools like Canva or LogoMakr on a smartphone. Choose 2-3 colors that stand out. For example, orange and green for fruits, or red and yellow for vegetables. Use a simple symbol: a mango, a leaf, or a sun. Keep it clean and recognizable even when small. A good logo works in black and white too. Once designed, save it as a PNG with transparent background. You can print it on stickers or directly on pouches. For packaging, you can order custom printed pouches with your logo from suppliers like Alibaba or local printers. Minimum order is often 1000 pieces, costing $0.15 to $0.30 each. If that's too expensive, buy plain pouches and stick on printed labels. A roll of 500 labels with your logo costs $10 to $20. Your brand name and logo should appear on every package, your social media, and your business card. Consistency builds trust. Tell a story: "Our mangoes are sun-dried in Ghana by local farmers." This adds value. Also, consider trademarking your logo if you plan to export. For now, focus on a simple, attractive design that reflects your product's quality. A strong brand can let you charge 10-20% more than unbranded products. So invest a little time and money in a name and logo that customers will remember.

lessons.title: Creating Product Labels with Ingredients and Dates
lessons.body: A product label is a legal and practical requirement. It tells customers what they are buying and how to use it. For dried fruits and vegetables, your label must include: product name, ingredients (if any added), net weight, production date, expiry date, and your contact information. If you add sugar, sulphur dioxide, or preservatives, list them. For example: "Ingredients: Dried mango, sugar (5%), sulphur dioxide (preservative)." If no additives, write "Ingredients: Dried mango." Net weight: weigh your product accurately. Use a digital kitchen scale ($10-$20). Fill the pouch, then weigh. For a 100g pack, the net weight should be exactly 100g. Don't include the packaging weight. Production date: write the date you dried and packaged. Expiry date: add 6-12 months depending on moisture and packaging. For example, if production is 01/06/2025, expiry could be 01/06/2026. Use a clear format: DD/MM/YYYY. For local sales, you can handwrite dates with a permanent marker, but printed labels look more professional. You can buy blank sticker sheets and print at a local cyber cafe for $0.05 per label. Or use a label maker. Include storage instructions: "Store in a cool, dry place. Reseal after opening." Also add your phone number and location. This helps with traceability and reorders. For export, you need more: batch number, nutrition facts, country of origin, and importer details. But start simple. Always double-check dates and weights. A mislabeled product can lead to customer complaints or legal issues. Also, use food-grade ink if printing directly on packaging. For small-scale, stickers are safest. Labeling also helps you manage inventory: you know which batch to sell first. So make labeling a habit. It shows professionalism and builds customer confidence.

lessons.title: Packaging for Different Markets: Local, Urban, Export
lessons.body: Different markets need different packaging. For local markets (village markets, small shops), customers want small quantities and low prices. Use clear poly bags of 50g or 100g. They cost $0.02 to $0.05 each. You can sell a 50g pack for $0.50. Packaging should be simple: a clear bag with a small sticker showing your brand and expiry date. No need for fancy printing. For urban markets (supermarkets, health shops), customers want convenience and trust. Use stand-up pouches with zip locks or laminated pouches. Sizes: 100g, 200g, 500g. These cost $0.20 to $0.50 each. You need a printed label with barcode, nutrition facts, and a nice design. Urban customers will pay $2 to $5 for a 200g pack. You may need to register with the local food authority, like NAFDAC in Nigeria or KEBS in Kenya. For export markets (Europe, USA, Middle East), requirements are strict. You need food-grade packaging that meets FDA or EU standards. Use high-barrier foil pouches or vacuum-sealed bags. Labels must be in English and the destination language, with all allergen info, nutrition facts, and traceability. You also need a barcode (UPC or EAN). Packaging costs $0.50 to $1.00 per unit. You must comply with labeling laws, like including the importer's address. Export also requires bulk packaging for shipping: use cartons with liners. For example, 10kg of dried mango in a foil bag inside a carton. Always test your packaging for moisture and insect resistance. For local, you can use simple bags; for urban, invest in better pouches; for export, follow international standards. Start with local, then upgrade as you grow. Each market has different price points, so adjust your packaging and pricing accordingly.

lessons.title: Using Eco-Friendly and Recyclable Packaging
lessons.body: More customers, especially in urban areas and export markets, prefer eco-friendly packaging. This can also reduce your environmental impact. Common options include: kraft paper bags, biodegradable plastic bags (made from corn starch), and glass jars. Kraft paper bags with a inner lining of wax or PLA (plant-based plastic) are affordable. A pack of 100 paper bags with window costs $5 to $10. They are recyclable and compostable. However, they may not keep products as fresh as foil pouches. Use them for short shelf life (3-6 months) or for products that will be eaten quickly. Biodegradable plastic bags look like regular plastic but break down in 6-12 months. They cost $0.05 to $0.15 each, about twice the price of regular plastic. You can find them from suppliers in South Africa or online. Glass jars are reusable and recyclable, but heavy and breakable. They are good for gift packs. For labels, use recycled paper stickers and soy-based ink. Also, avoid over-packaging: use the smallest bag that fits your product. For export, eco-friendly packaging can be a selling point. For example, "Packaged in compostable bags." You can also offer a refill option: customers bring their own containers and you sell in bulk. This reduces packaging waste. Another idea: use banana leaves or woven baskets for local markets, but ensure food safety. Always check that eco-friendly packaging is food-grade. Some biodegradable bags may not be airtight, so add a moisture absorber sachet. Test shelf life: if you switch from plastic to paper, check after one month for mold. If you see any, go back to plastic or add a barrier layer. Eco-friendly packaging may cost more, but you can charge a premium. Many customers are willing to pay 10-20% more for sustainable products. So consider it as an investment in your brand image and the planet.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Packaging & Branding for African Dried Fruit and Vegetable Businesses

Packaging is not a cost centre â it is your cheapest salesperson. In dried fruit and vegetable processing, packaging determines whether your product survives the journey to market, whether a retailer trusts you enough to stock it, and whether a customer picks your brand over the unlabelled heap next to it. Across Africa, where cold chains are limited and transport is rough, packaging also decides whether your dried mango arrives as a premium snack or as a sticky, mouldy loss.

This practical reference pulls together the six lessons in this module into one working document. Use it as a bench guide while you source materials, price your unit, and design your brand. It is written for small and medium processors in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and similar markets â businesses that need to move from selling in open basins to selling sealed, labelled, repeat-purchase products.

1. Choosing affordable and attractive packaging

The core trade-off is barrier performance versus unit cost. Dried products are hygroscopic: they pull moisture from the air, which reactivates enzymes and mould. Your packaging must block moisture, oxygen and light, and resist puncturing in transit. The cheapest material that does all three for your specific product and shelf-life target wins.

For most African small processors, the practical answer is a metallised PET or PET/PE laminate pouch for retail, and food-grade LDPE or PP bags for bulk and local wholesale. Laminate pouches cost more per unit but let you claim 6â12 months shelf life, which is what urban supermarkets and export buyers demand. Plain LDPE gives you weeks, not months.

Table 1: Indicative packaging cost and performance by format (2024 estimates, East/West Africa)
Format Typical unit cost (USD) Moisture barrier Best market Typical shelf life
Clear LDPE bag, 500 g0.02â0.05LowLocal market, same-week sale2â6 weeks
PP stand-up pouch, 200 g0.06â0.12MediumUrban retail, informal supermarkets3â6 months
Metallised PET/PE pouch, 100 g0.10â0.20HighSupermarkets, urban premium9â12 months
Foil laminate pouch, 100 g0.18â0.35Very highExport, e-commerce12â18 months
Rigid PET jar with lid, 250 g0.25â0.45HighGifting, premium urban9â12 months

Sources: Author's synthesis of supplier quotations from packaging distributors in Nairobi, Lagos and Accra (2024); FAO (2007) Packaging for Fruit and Vegetables; ITC (2021) Packaging for Export technical notes.

2. Sealing and labelling for longer shelf life

A perfect pouch with a bad seal is a failed product. Heat sealing is the standard: you need consistent temperature, pressure and dwell time. Impulse sealers (cheap, common in African workshops) work for LDPE and PP but struggle with thick laminates. For laminates, use a constant-heat band sealer or a vacuum sealer with a wide seal bar. Always seal through a clean, dry surface â product crumbs or oil in the seal zone create channels for moisture.

Nitrogen flushing or vacuum packing removes oxygen, slowing oxidation of fats and preserving colour in products like dried mango, tomato and pineapple. For export, vacuum or nitrogen-flushed foil laminates are the norm.

Labelling is a legal and commercial tool. At minimum, your label must carry: product name, net weight, ingredient list, production and expiry dates, batch/lot code, storage instructions, and your business name and contact. In Kenya, KEBS and the Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances Act govern this; in Nigeria, NAFDAC; in Ghana, FDA Ghana. Export markets add country-of-origin, allergen and nutrition labelling requirements.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Food safety and legal compliance

Never use non-food-grade inks, adhesives or recycled containers that previously held chemicals, pesticides or petroleum products. Printing directly onto food-contact surfaces with standard inks can leach toxins. Always use food-grade packaging certified by your national standards body (KEBS, NAFDAC, FDA Ghana, UNBS, TBS). Incorrectly labelled products can be seized, fined or destroyed, and a single food safety incident can end a young brand. If you cannot afford compliant packaging, sell in bulk to a licensed packer rather than risk your business and your customers' health.

3. Designing a simple brand name and logo

Your brand must be easy to say, easy to remember, and easy to spell in the languages your customers use. Avoid generic names like "Quality Dried Fruits" â they cannot be protected and do not differentiate. A strong name often draws on origin (a region, a river, a mountain), a benefit, or a founder story. Check availability with your national trademark registry and domain registrar before printing thousands of labels.

Your logo should work in one colour, at small sizes, and on a plain background. A simple wordmark plus a single icon (a leaf, a sun, a fruit silhouette) is enough. Resist complexity: it raises print cost and fails on cheap flexographic labels. Use a consistent colour palette â two colours maximum for cost control â and repeat it across every product so retailers and customers recognise you instantly.

4. Creating product labels with ingredients and dates

Ingredient lists must be in descending order by weight. If your product is 100% dried mango with no additives, state "Ingredients: Dried mango (100%)". If you add sugar, sulphur dioxide (common preservative for colour retention) or citric acid, list them. Sulphites are a declared allergen in many markets â critical for export.

Dates matter commercially and legally. Print production date (MFG) and expiry/best-before date (EXP/BB) clearly, plus a batch code that lets you trace a problem back to a specific drying run. Use a date coder or pre-printed labels; handwritten dates look unprofessional and are easily altered, which erodes retailer trust.

Table 2: Minimum label information by market
Label element Local market Urban retail (KEBS/NAFDAC/FDA) Export (EU/US)
Product nameRequiredRequiredRequired
Net weightRecommendedRequiredRequired (metric + imperial for US)
Ingredient listRecommendedRequiredRequired, allergens highlighted
Production & expiry dateRecommendedRequiredRequired (best-before format)
Batch/lot codeOptionalRequiredRequired for traceability
Storage instructionsOptionalRequiredRequired
Business name & addressRecommendedRequiredRequired (importer address for EU)
Nutrition declarationNot requiredIncreasingly requiredRequired (EU Reg. 1169/2011; US FDA)
Country of originOptionalRecommendedRequired

Sources: Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) labelling requirements; NAFDAC Nigeria food labelling regulations; FDA Ghana guidelines; European Union Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on food information to consumers; US FDA Food Labeling Guide.

5. Packaging for different markets: local, urban, export

Local markets reward low cost and familiar formats. Small sachets (20â50 g) at low price points move fast. Packaging can be simple, but it must still protect the product. Many local buyers repackage, so bulk 5â10 kg food-grade bags are common.

Urban retail rewards presentation and trust. Stand-up pouches with clear windows, clean typography, a visible brand and a barcode (EAN-13) are expected. Supermarkets require barcodes for scanning; without one, you cannot get on shelf. Shelf life claims must be honest and supported by your sealing and storage.

Export rewards compliance above all. You need food-grade laminate packaging, full traceability, compliant labelling in the destination language, and often certification (HACCP, organic, Fairtrade). Export packaging is a capital cost, not a marketing cost â budget for it before you sign a buyer contract.

6. Using eco-friendly and recyclable packaging

Sustainability is now a purchasing criterion in urban African markets and a hard requirement in many export markets. Options include kraft paper/PLA laminates, mono-material PE pouches (recyclable in some systems), and reusable glass jars. Be honest: a "100% recyclable" claim that your local waste system cannot process is greenwashing and can attract regulatory attention.

Practical low-cost moves: reduce packaging weight, use recycled-content outer cartons, offer refill or bulk options, and print with water-based inks. Where recyclable laminates cost more, calculate the premium against the price uplift you can charge and the export access you gain. For many African processors, the winning strategy is a recyclable mono-material pouch for the local/urban line and a certified compostable or recyclable format for export.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm packaging is food-grade and certified by your national standards body.
  • â Match barrier level to your target shelf life and market (LDPE for local, laminate for export).
  • â Test your seal: squeeze, water-bath and 48-hour humidity check before scaling up.
  • â Include product name, net weight, ingredients, MFG/EXP dates, batch code, storage and contact.
  • â Check trademark and domain availability before printing labels.
  • â Keep logo to one colour and two brand colours to control print cost.
  • â Add an EAN-13 barcode before approaching supermarkets.
  • â Verify destination-market labelling rules before any export shipment.

Further Reading (free official sources)

  1. FAO â Packaging for Fruit and Vegetables (Agricultural Services Bulletin 155)
  2. FAO â Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing and Products
  3. International Trade Centre (ITC) â Packaging and export market guides
  4. Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â Standards and labelling requirements
  5. NAFDAC Nigeria â Food registration and labelling guidelines

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills course Dried Fruit & Vegetable Processing. Always verify current regulatory requirements with your national standards authority before commercial production or export.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of affordable clear plastic bags used for dried products?
quiz.explanation: Clear poly bags of 0.05mm to 0.08mm thickness are common and affordable for local markets.

quiz.q: Which packaging type is best for long shelf life of 6-12 months?
options: B) Laminated pouches with foil layer
quiz.explanation: Laminated pouches with a foil or metallized layer provide a barrier against moisture and air, extending shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce packaging cost per unit?
quiz.explanation: Buying packaging materials in bulk (e.g., 5000 pouches) can reduce the unit cost by about 30%.

quiz.q: Which size of packaging is most common for local markets?
quiz.explanation: Smaller sizes like 50g and 100g sell faster in low-income areas because they are affordable.

quiz.q: What should you do before sealing a bag of dried fruit?
options: B) Ensure product is cool and dry
D) Leave it open for a day
quiz.explanation: Sealing while hot can cause condensation; the product must be cool and dry to prevent mold.

quiz.q: What is the recommended heat setting for sealing poly bags with an impulse sealer?
quiz.explanation: For poly bags, a medium heat of 2-3 seconds is usually sufficient for a good seal.

quiz.q: Which of the following must be included on a product label?
options: B) Production date and expiry date
quiz.explanation: Production and expiry dates are essential for food safety and customer trust.

quiz.q: How long can dried mango at 10% moisture last in a foil pouch?
quiz.explanation: Properly dried and sealed in a foil pouch, dried mango can last up to 12 months.

quiz.q: Why is labeling important for traceability?
options: A) It helps you track batches for quality control
B) It makes the package heavier
C) It is required by law in all countries
quiz.explanation: Labeling with batch numbers and dates allows you to trace and recall products if needed.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when sealing and labeling?
options: A) Seal immediately after drying while still warm
B) Work in a humid room
C) Wear gloves and work in a dry room
D) Use recycled plastic with odors
quiz.explanation: Wearing gloves and working in a dry room prevents contamination and moisture absorption.

quiz.q: What is a key characteristic of a good brand name?
options: B) Easy to remember and pronounce
quiz.explanation: A simple, memorable name helps customers recall and recommend your product.

quiz.q: Which free tool can be used to design a simple logo?
quiz.explanation: Canva is a free, user-friendly design tool available on smartphones and computers.

quiz.q: What is the typical minimum order for custom printed pouches?
quiz.explanation: Most suppliers require a minimum order of 1000 pieces for custom printed pouches.

quiz.q: How much more can a strong brand let you charge compared to unbranded products?
quiz.explanation: A well-known brand can command a premium of 10-20% over unbranded competitors.

quiz.q: What should be listed under 'Ingredients' on a label?
options: B) All added substances like sugar or preservatives
quiz.explanation: All ingredients, including additives, must be declared for transparency and safety.

quiz.q: What is the correct format for dates on a label?
quiz.explanation: DD/MM/YYYY is commonly used and clear for most customers.

quiz.q: Why is net weight important on a label?
options: A) It tells the customer the exact amount of product
B) It makes the package look heavier
C) It is only for export
quiz.explanation: Net weight informs the customer of the actual product quantity, excluding packaging.

quiz.q: What is a good storage instruction to include on a label?
options: A) Store in a cool, dry place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry conditions help maintain crispness and prevent mold.

quiz.q: For local markets, what packaging is most suitable?
quiz.explanation: Clear poly bags are affordable and practical for small-scale local sales.

quiz.q: What extra feature do urban customers often prefer?
quiz.explanation: Zip locks provide convenience for resealing and are popular in urban markets.

quiz.q: What is required for export packaging that is not needed for local?
quiz.explanation: Export markets require barcodes (UPC/EAN) for tracking and retail.

quiz.q: What is a common certification needed for export to Europe?
quiz.explanation: EU organic certification is often required for organic dried fruits exported to Europe.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using eco-friendly packaging?
options: B) It can attract environmentally conscious customers
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Eco-friendly packaging appeals to customers who value sustainability, often allowing a premium price.

quiz.q: Which material is biodegradable?
quiz.explanation: PLA is made from renewable resources like corn starch and is biodegradable.

quiz.q: What should you check when switching to paper bags?
quiz.explanation: Paper bags may not provide a good moisture barrier, so test shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a refill option?
options: A) Selling in bulk to customers who bring containers
quiz.explanation: Refill reduces packaging waste by letting customers reuse their own containers.

quiz.q: What can you add to eco-friendly packaging to extend shelf life?
quiz.explanation: A moisture absorber helps control humidity inside the package.

quiz.q: How much more are customers willing to pay for sustainable products?
quiz.explanation: Many customers will pay a 10-20% premium for eco-friendly products.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using biodegradable bags?
quiz.explanation: Some biodegradable bags are not airtight, so they may require additional barrier layers.

quiz.q: What should you do before sealing a bag with a zip lock?
options: A) Ensure the zip is clean and free of product
quiz.explanation: Any product stuck in the zip can prevent a proper seal, leading to moisture entry.
